**Q.** What is ResStock, and which figures did it produce?

**A.** ResStock is the End-Use Load Profiles dataset produced by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), the U.S. Department of Energy's primary laboratory for energy efficiency and renewable energy research [@nrel_EndUseLoadProfiles_2024; @nrel_ResStock20242Release_2024]. I used the 2024.2 release of the dataset.

ResStock models a statistically representative sample of the U.S. housing stock. Each modeled dwelling has physical characteristics — square footage, insulation levels, HVAC equipment, and local climate — drawn from federal survey data. Its energy consumption is simulated hour-by-hour using the DOE's EnergyPlus building energy simulation engine. For each home, ResStock provides a baseline scenario (with the home's existing heating system) and a heat pump retrofit scenario (in which the home is equipped with a cold-climate air-source heat pump), each with a complete 8,760-hour energy consumption profile covering electricity, natural gas, heating oil, and propane.

Before running the bill analysis, I applied two corrections to ResStock's simulated load curves.

First, a **multifamily non-HVAC electricity correction.** ResStock systematically overstates electricity consumption for multifamily buildings, driven by inflated non-HVAC end uses (plug loads, lighting, appliances). The overstatement grows with a utility's share of multifamily housing. I corrected this by scaling each multifamily building's non-HVAC electricity consumption to match the single-family per-square-foot benchmark for each end use. HVAC loads were left unchanged.

Second, an **air-leakage (ACH50) infiltration correction.** ResStock assigns building air-leakage rates from a database that systematically overestimates infiltration relative to field measurements, inflating simulated heating and cooling loads [@chan_AnalysisAirLeakage_2013a]. I corrected this by benchmarking each building's assigned air-leakage rate against the empirical regression of Chan et al., which predicts expected leakage from housing characteristics (vintage, climate zone, floor area, building height), and scaling HVAC loads proportionally within each heating-type group (heat pump, electric resistance, natural gas, delivered fuels). The correction applies to electric heating, gas heating, and electric cooling loads. Non-HVAC loads were unaffected.

I used ResStock for the population-level bill-change analysis, in which I computed total energy bills for each of the `{python} f"{b.n_resstock_bldgs:,}"` BGE-territory buildings, under both their baseline heating system and a heat pump retrofit, and reported the share of households whose bills would increase or decrease. These results appear in @fig-bill-change-quadrants-default-natgas, @fig-bill-change-quadrants-default-delivered, @fig-bill-change-quadrants-rate-comparison-natgas, and @fig-bill-change-quadrants-rate-comparison-delivered. I used CAIRO — the Customer Affordability, Incentives, and Rates Optimization model, a rate simulation engine developed by the National Laboratory of the Rockies (formerly NREL) [@nrel_CustomerAffordabilityIncentives_2026] — to compute each building's electricity bills. CAIRO takes a building's hourly electricity load profile and a tariff structure as inputs, and computes the resulting bill, including fixed charges, volumetric charges, and demand charges where applicable.

For the natgas and delivered subpopulation charts (@fig-total-bill-before-after-natgas, @fig-total-bill-before-after-delivered, @fig-total-bill-3bar-natgas, and @fig-total-bill-3bar-delivered), both the electric and fossil fuel portions derive from ResStock consumption data, with electric bills computed by CAIRO. The representative-home analysis in Section III uses the Company data described above.

<br>

**Q.** What fossil fuel price data did you use?

**A.** For natural gas, I applied the rates from BGE's gas Schedule D tariff to each household's monthly gas consumption from ResStock. For heating oil and propane, I used the U.S. Energy Information Administration's monthly residential price series [@eia_HeatingOilPropanePrices_2024]. These fuel prices appear in all figures that show total energy bills: @fig-total-bill-before-after-natgas and @fig-total-bill-3bar-natgas (natural gas component), @fig-total-bill-before-after-delivered and @fig-total-bill-3bar-delivered (oil and propane components), and the population bill-change charts @fig-bill-change-quadrants-default-natgas, @fig-bill-change-quadrants-default-delivered, @fig-bill-change-quadrants-rate-comparison-natgas, and @fig-bill-change-quadrants-rate-comparison-delivered.


### Methodology

#### Representative home profiles {#sec-method-profiles}

<br>

**Q.** How did you construct the before-and-after electricity consumption profiles used in Section III?

**A.** I used BGE's residential electricity consumption data, provided in discovery, which contains hourly and monthly kWh broken down by electric-heating and non-electric-heating customers.

For the **"before" profile** — representing a typical home that heats with fossil fuels — I computed a representative home by averaging the electricity consumption of BGE's non-electric-heating residential customers (Schedules R and RL, excluding the electric-heating subpopulation). This population includes all residential customers whose primary heating system is natural gas, oil, propane, or another non-electric fuel.

For the **"after" profile** — representing a typical home after installing a heat pump — I computed a representative home by averaging the electricity consumption of BGE's electric-heating residential customers (Schedules RH and RLH).

These profiles are averages across two different customer populations, not measurements of the same homes tracked before and after a retrofit. I am comparing the typical electricity consumption pattern of fossil-fuel-heated customers to the typical electricity consumption pattern of electrically heated customers. This is a proxy for the change in load associated with electrifying a home's heating system, not a perfectly isolated measurement of the effect of heat pump adoption on a single home.

I used heating versus non-heating subclass data because that is the finest granularity the Company could provide. BGE's residential subclass designations distinguish only "heating" from "non-heating" loads — they do not identify which customers have heat pumps.[^ccandr-heating-only] The Company confirmed in discovery that it "does not track customers by known heat source" and has not performed any analysis of heat pump customer costs or load profiles.[^ccandr-no-hp-tracking] The electric-heating subclass (Schedules RH and RLH) therefore includes both heat pump and electric resistance customers. This means the "after" profile reflects a mix of heating technologies, not heat pumps alone.

[^ccandr-heating-only]: CCANDR01-01: "These designations are only at the heating/non-heating level and do not indicate if a customer has a heat pump or indicate a heat pump type."

[^ccandr-no-hp-tracking]: CCANDR01-03, CCANDR01-08, CCANDR01-09 (BGE "does not track customers by known heat source"); CCANDR01-01, CCANDR01-05, CCANDR01-07 (BGE has not analyzed heat pump customer costs or load profiles).

For the monthly consumption totals that drive the bill calculations and monthly load profile charts, I used BGE's monthly residential customer counts and kilowatt-hour sales for the test year April 2025 through March 2026. For the hourly consumption patterns, I used BGE's hourly residential kilowatt-hour data for calendar year 2024 (from CCANDR 1-11, Attachment 1), which was the most recent year for which the Company could provide study-quality hourly data.

#### Hourly marginal delivery costs {#sec-method-mc}

<br>

**Q.** Can you walk through how you computed the hourly bulk transmission marginal costs shown in @fig-mc-heatmap-bulk-tx?

**A.** Yes. The calculation has four steps.

**Step 1: Annual transmission cost per kilowatt.** I used the PJM Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS) rate for the BGE transmission zone [@pjm_NetworkIntegrationTransmission_2025]. The NITS rate is the zone's Annual Transmission Revenue Requirement divided by its billing determinants, and it is what every load-serving entity in the BGE zone actually pays PJM for each kilowatt of network service. For 2025, BGE's zonal revenue requirement was approximately `$358` million as of January 1 and approximately `$400` million as of June 1, producing NITS rates of `$55.85`/kW-year and `$59.07`/kW-year respectively [@pjm_NetworkIntegrationTransmission_2025].

**Step 2: Day-weighted blending.** PJM published two NITS rates for 2025, one effective January 1 and one effective June 1, so neither rate covers the full calendar year. I weighted each by the number of days it was in effect — 151 days at the January rate and 214 days at the June rate — giving a 2025 effective rate of approximately `$57.74`/kW-year. No inflation adjustment is required, because the NITS rate is already stated in current-year dollars.

The NITS rate is an embedded average cost — it reflects the revenue requirement on PJM's existing transmission plant, not a purely forward-looking long-run marginal cost. I use it because no better estimate is available. E3 used the same rate as its transmission capacity value in the avoided-cost study the Illinois Commerce Commission commissioned, after both PJM and MISO advised that they could not provide a more accurate marginal cost for transmission capacity and lacked the data infrastructure to support an independent calculation [@debenedictis_ValueCompensationDistributed_2025].[^e3-nits-proxy]

[^e3-nits-proxy]: E3, *ICC-VDER Report*, § 6.1.2: the Network Transmission Service rates used as a proxy for transmission avoided costs "are more indicative of an average cost of capacity rather than a marginal cost," a limitation both RTOs acknowledged while confirming they had no better estimate to offer.

**Step 3: Peak-hour identification.** Additional consumption drives new transmission investment only when the system is near its limits, so the annual cost belongs in those hours and not in the rest of the year. I loaded BGE zonal hourly load for calendar year 2025 from PJM Data Miner 2 [@pjm_DataMiner2Metered_2025], ranked all 8,760 hours by load, and selected the top 150 hours as the constrained hours. I used 150 hours, and applied no seasonal restriction, to follow E3's ICC-VDER methodology, which allocates transmission and distribution capacity costs across the top 150 load hours of the full year [@debenedictis_ValueCompensationDistributed_2025].

**Step 4: Load-weighted allocation.** I allocated the annual cost across those 150 hours in proportion to each hour's load, using the Peak Capacity Allocation Factor described in Appendix C of E3's ICC-VDER report: each hour's factor is its "share of load in each of these hours divided by the total load across these 150 top load hours" [@debenedictis_ValueCompensationDistributed_2025]:

$$
PCAF_h = \frac{L_h}{\sum_{k \in \text{top-150}} L_k}
$$

Multiplying the `$57.74`/kW-year figure by each hour's factor produces that hour's marginal cost in dollars per kilowatt-hour. The remaining 8,610 hours receive a marginal cost of zero. The hourly values sum to the annual rate, which I verified programmatically. The resulting hourly profile is @fig-mc-heatmap-bulk-tx.

<br>

**Q.** Can you walk through how you computed the hourly distribution marginal costs shown in @fig-mc-heatmap-dist-sub-tx?

**A.** Yes. The calculation follows the same four steps, with a different cost input and a narrower peak window:

**Step 1: Annualized avoided cost.** I started with the Brattle Group's avoided distribution cost of $32/kW-year (in 2022 dollars), from BGE's direct testimony in Case No. 9692.[^brattle-dist] This figure represents the per-kilowatt replacement value of BGE's distribution system — including 34 kV sub-transmission, 13 kV primary, and secondary voltage levels — levelized with a 12% economic carrying charge. It captures the forward-looking cost of distribution capacity: the annual cost of adding one kilowatt of new distribution capacity to serve incremental load.

**Step 2: CPI inflation.** I adjusted the 2022-dollar figure to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index [@fred_ConsumerPriceIndexAll_2025], yielding approximately $36/kW-year.

**Step 3: Peak-hour identification.** I loaded BGE's hourly demand profile for calendar year 2025 from PJM Data Miner 2 [@pjm_DataMiner2Metered_2025], ranked all 8,760 hours by BGE zone load in descending order, and selected the top 100 hours as the constrained hours — the hours during which additional demand is most likely to trigger new distribution capacity investment.

**Step 4: Load-weighted allocation.** For each of the 100 peak hours, I computed a weight equal to that hour's load divided by the sum of load across all 100 peak hours:

$$
PCAF_h = \frac{L_h}{\sum_{k \in \text{top-100}} L_k}
$$

I then multiplied the annualized cost (~$36/kW-year) by each hour's weight to produce a $/kWh marginal cost for that hour. All non-peak hours receive a marginal cost of zero. The sum of all 8,760 hourly values equals the original $/kW-year figure — a property I verified programmatically. The resulting hourly profile is @fig-mc-heatmap-dist-sub-tx.

#### Incremental cost and overpayment {#sec-method-incremental}

<br>

**Q.** How did you compute the incremental T&D cost of heat pump adoption?

**A.** By "new T&D costs," I mean the forward-looking marginal costs that the transmission and distribution system incurs because of the customer's heat pump installation — the cost of capacity expansion triggered by additional consumption during the constrained hours identified in the preceding answer.

I multiplied the representative home's hourly electricity consumption by the hourly marginal-cost schedule described above, and summed across all 8,760 hours to get the total annual marginal T&D cost for that home. I performed this calculation for both the "before" and "after" consumption profiles. The difference between the two annual totals is the incremental marginal T&D cost attributable to the shift from fossil fuel heating to electric heating — the `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_mc_delivery_after - r.all_fossil_annual_mc_delivery_before)` figure I cited in Section III.

<br>

**Q.** How do you define the overpayment caused by heat pump adoption?

**A.** Overpayment is the increase in a customer's payments that exceeds the increase in costs caused by the customer's heat pump adoption.

For transmission and distribution, I calculate the change in the customer's annual T&D charges (the charges paid using the "after" consumption profile minus the charges paid using the "before" profile) and subtract the incremental T&D cost described above. The remainder is the **T&D overpayment**:

$$
\text{T\&D overpayment}
=
\text{increase in T\&D charges}
-
\text{increase in marginal T\&D costs}.
$$

I also include the increase in EmPOWER contributions. As I established in Section III, EmPOWER costs are unrelated to customer usage, so the customer's entire increase in EmPOWER payments is included in the overpayment.

The total overpayment is therefore:

$$
\text{total overpayment}
=
\left(
\text{increase in T\&D charges}
-
\text{increase in marginal T\&D costs}
\right)
+
\text{increase in EmPOWER contributions}.
$$

For the representative home in my analysis, the result is an annual overpayment of `{python} dollar(r.all_fossil_annual_total_overcharge)`.

#### Schedule R-HP rate derivation {#sec-method-rhp}

<br>

**Q.** How did you derive the proposed Schedule R-HP rates shown in Section V?

**A.** For each bill component — distribution, transmission, and EmPOWER Maryland — I first computed the representative home's annual bill under BGE's filed monthly rates, for both the "before" and "after" consumption profiles. The bill calculations use the Company's actual filed monthly rates (which vary slightly across the test year), applied to each profile's monthly kWh.

I then defined the **fair annual bill** for each component — the amount the customer should pay after installing a heat pump:

- For **distribution and transmission**, the fair annual bill equals the pre-installation bill plus the incremental marginal cost caused by the heat pump: $\text{fair bill} = \text{bill}_{\text{before}} + \Delta MC$. This allows the customer's bill to increase by exactly the amount of new T&D costs their heat pump causes, and no more.
- For **EmPOWER Maryland**, the fair annual bill equals the pre-installation bill: $\text{fair bill} = \text{bill}_{\text{before}}$. The customer's EmPOWER contributions stay flat.
- **Generation** is unchanged.

The Schedule R-HP rate for each component is then a derived quantity: I divided the fair annual bill by the representative home's post-installation annual kWh to obtain a cents-per-kWh rate:

$$
\text{rate}_{\text{R-HP}} = \frac{\text{fair bill}}{\text{kWh}_{\text{after}}}
$$

The cents/kWh figures in the rate comparison table in Section V are annual-average effective rates — each component's annual bill divided by annual kWh — not filed tariff line items. The underlying bill calculations use BGE's actual filed monthly rates.

This is a representative-home calculation. It determines the rate at which the average fossil-fuel-heated home, after installing a heat pump, would pay no more than its cost of service for each component.

#### Fixed-charge alternative {#sec-method-fixed-charge}

<br>

**Q.** In Section X, you testified that eliminating the heat pump overpayment within Schedule R would require reducing the distribution, transmission, and EmPOWER Maryland volumetric rates by approximately `{python} pct(fc.volumetric_rate_reduction)` and raising the average monthly fixed charge from `{python} dollar(fc.original_fixed_charge, accuracy=2)` to `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge, accuracy=2)`. How did you calculate those figures?

**A.** I solved for the version of Schedule R that satisfies two conditions at the same time.

The first condition is **cost reflectivity**. When a home switches from fossil fuel heating to electric heating, the increase in the volumetric charges it pays must equal the increase in marginal transmission and distribution costs that the switch causes. I applied the redesign to three volumetric charges — distribution, transmission, and EmPOWER Maryland — and scaled all three by a single uniform factor, which preserves each charge's existing month-to-month shape. I did not change generation charges.

The second condition is **revenue neutrality**. The revenue held constant is the revenue collected through the charges the redesign touches: the monthly customer charge plus the three targeted volumetric charges. Generation revenue is unaffected by the redesign and therefore does not enter the calculation on either side. Whatever revenue the reduction in the targeted volumetric rates gives up must come back through the fixed charge.

<br>

**Q.** How did you determine the factor by which the targeted volumetric rates would have to fall?

**A.** That factor follows directly from the cost-reflectivity condition, and it does not depend on the fixed charge at all. Because the same default rate applies to the home both before and after it installs a heat pump, the identical fixed charge is paid in both cases and cancels out of the before-and-after bill difference. Only the targeted volumetric charges change.

The inputs are the same figures I presented in Section III. Under the rates as filed, the increase in the representative home's targeted volumetric charges is `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_incremental_variable_charge)` per year — `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_incremental_td_charge)` in distribution and transmission charges and `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_incremental_empower_charge)` in EmPOWER contributions. The increase in marginal T&D cost that the same change in consumption causes is `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_incremental_marginal_cost)` per year. The difference between the two is the `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_overpayment)` annual overpayment.

Aligning the two follows directly from those two numbers. Multiplying the monthly volumetric charges by the ratio of the incremental cost to the incremental charges — `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_incremental_marginal_cost)` divided by `{python} dollar(fc.retrofit_incremental_variable_charge)` — scales the increase down by that same ratio, leaving it equal to the incremental cost. That ratio is therefore the scaling factor the redesign requires:

$$
\lambda^{*}
=
\frac{\Delta MC_{\text{T\&D}}}
{\Delta V_{\text{T\&D + EmPOWER}}}
$$

For BGE, that ratio is `{python} pct(fc.implied_lambda, accuracy=1)`. In other words, the targeted volumetric rates would have to be cut to roughly one-tenth of their filed levels — a reduction of approximately `{python} pct(fc.volumetric_rate_reduction)` — before a home switching to electric heating would pay no more than the additional T&D costs it causes. I apply this ratio only to the T&D and EmPOWER Maryland portion of the bill, leaving generation charges unchanged.

<br>

**Q.** How did you then determine the fixed charge?

**A.** From the revenue neutrality condition. Cutting the three targeted volumetric rates to `{python} pct(fc.implied_lambda, accuracy=1)` of their filed levels leaves the remaining `{python} pct(fc.volumetric_rate_reduction)` of the revenue those charges collect to be recovered elsewhere, and the only remaining place to recover it in this exercise is the fixed charge.

Using BGE's actual residential customer counts and kilowatt-hour sales, the three targeted charges collect approximately `{python} dollar(fc.class_variable_revenue_per_customer)` per residential customer per year across the class as a whole. The redesign removes approximately `{python} dollar(fc.class_variable_revenue_per_customer * fc.volumetric_rate_reduction)` of that amount per customer per year. Spread across twelve monthly bills, replacing it requires raising the fixed charge by `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge_delta, accuracy=2)` per month:

$$
F^{*}
=
F_{0}
+
\frac{\left(1 - \lambda^{*}\right) V_{\text{class}}}
{12 \, N_{\text{class}}}
$$

where $F_{0}$ is the current fixed charge, $V_{\text{class}}$ is the annual revenue the targeted volumetric charges collect from the residential class, and $N_{\text{class}}$ is the number of residential customers. Starting from BGE's current Schedule R customer charge of `{python} dollar(fc.original_fixed_charge, accuracy=2)` per month, the result is a fixed charge of `{python} dollar(fc.fixed_charge, accuracy=2)` per month.[^fixed-charge-baseline]

[^fixed-charge-baseline]: I use BGE's filed Schedule R customer charge of $10.00 per month as the starting point. Adding the Universal Service Program charge and weighting by the Company's actual monthly customer counts produces an average fixed charge of approximately $10.06 per month; the distinction does not affect the magnitude of the result.
